burton_span.exact: that fuliginous exhalation of corrupt seed, troubling the brain, heart and mind; the brain I say, not in essence, but by consent

1.3.2.4-f43.text: Ex menstrui sanguinis tetra ad cor & cerebrum exhalatione, vitiatum semen mentem perturbat, &c., non per essentiam sed per consensum. Animus maerens & anxius inde malum trahit, & spiritus cerebrum obfuscantur, quae cuncta augentur, &c

translations.note: "spiritus cerebrum obfuscantur" does not parse as it stands. It probably means "spiritus cerebri" (the spirits of the brain are darkened) or "spiritus [et] cerebrum". The translation takes the second reading. "By consent" is the old medical idea of sympathy between organs: the brain suffers from a disorder in another part, not in its own substance. Both sentences break off at "&c."

burton_span.exact: that fuliginous exhalation of corrupt seed, troubling the brain, heart and mind; the brain I say, not in essence, but by consent

translations.text: From the foul exhalation of menstrual blood to the heart and brain, the corrupted seed disturbs the mind, etc., not in essence but by consent. The mind, grieving and anxious, draws harm from this, and the spirits and brain are darkened, all of which things are increased, etc.

translations.note: Per consensum: the old medical 'consent' (sympathy) between organs. The passage is cut with 'etc.' at several points; Burton's English at the anchor covers only the first part.
